fix(bot-desktop): a takeover counts as use of an idle screen

The idle stop times out a human lease nobody has used for four windows, judged by the screen's activity
stamp. A takeover did not stamp it; only the viewer's first RFB frame did. A takeover landing on a long-idle
screen while an idle check waited on start.lock was therefore read as an already abandoned lease: the
screen was stopped under the human who had just taken it, and their lease handed back to the agent.
display.lease.acquire now stamps activity before it writes the lease, as the idle section's comment already
said a takeover does: the new lease is visible to the screen's own idle check (and to this process's
listeners) from the moment it is written.

top_items.title: Hermes Agent ElevenLabs: Make Sound Effects With the Official Plugin
top_items.content:
Hermes Agent ElevenLabs support just got a new trick: Nous Research released an official plugin called elevenlabs-sound-effects that lets Hermes turn a short text description into a real sound effect. You type “a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall” and Hermes makes the audio file and sends it to you in chat. The plugin (v1.2.0) was added to the Hermes plugin catalog on 26 October 2026, and Nous announced it on X the next day as part of a growing set of “Game Dev Studio” tools for Hermes. Below I cover what it does, how to install it, every setting, what it costs to run, and how it fits next to the ElevenLabs voice you may already use in Hermes. I’ve also put one of my Hermes walkthrough videos below.

Key takeaways

One tool, elevenlabs_sound_effect: text in, sound file out (0.5 to 30 seconds, optional seamless loop).
Install with hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects.
Uses the same ELEVENLABS_API_KEY as Hermes’ ElevenLabs voice.
Ships a sound-design skill, a free local ffmpeg script and a Desktop sound library.

What the Hermes Agent ElevenLabs plugin does
The plugin connects Hermes to the ElevenLabs Sound Effects API. According to the catalog page, it adds exactly one tool to your agent: elevenlabs_sound_effect. You describe a sound in plain English and Hermes generates an audio file between 0.5 and 30 seconds long. It can also make the sound a seamless loop, which matters for things like background music, engine hums or rain.
Examples straight from the README:

“Glass shattering on a tile floor”
“A short retro coin pickup blip”
“90s hip-hop drum loop, 90 BPM, loopable”
“The sound of a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall”

Hermes picks the details for each sound itself: the description (up to 450 characters — longer prompts are refused before anything is sent), the length, whether it loops, and a prompt_influence value from 0 to 1. A higher value follows your words more literally; a lower one gives more variety. You can also ask for a specific model on a single sound.
It’s an Official plugin, maintained by NousResearch, listed under Tools, and it needs Hermes 0.22.0 or newer. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, and its only Python dependency is httpx, which Hermes already ships.
How to install the ElevenLabs plugin in Hermes
Installing takes one command. Here are the steps, in order:

Make sure you’re on Hermes 0.22.0 or later (hermes update if you’re not sure).
Run hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects. You can also install it straight from the hermes-official-plugins repo with hermes plugins install NousResearch/hermes-official-plugins#elevenlabs-sound-effects.
If ELEVENLABS_API_KEY isn’t set yet, the installer asks for it. You create a key in ElevenLabs under Profile → API keys.
The tool only shows up for the agent once the key is set.

Two details catch people out:

Plugins are per profile. If you run several Hermes profiles, install it on each one you want, for example hermes -p <profile> plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects.
Restricted keys need the right permission. If your ElevenLabs key is restricted, turn on the Sound Effects permission. It’s separate from the Text to Speech permission.

Prefer not to touch the terminal? Ask your agent: “Install the elevenlabs-sound-effects plugin on this profile and check the key works.”

Hermes ElevenLabs settings explained
In Hermes Desktop, open Capabilities → Plugins and click the gear icon on the plugin. Everywhere else, use hermes config set. These are the four settings the README lists:




Setting
Default
Options and notes




api_key
(unset)
Stored in .env as ELEVENLABS_API_KEY


sound_model
eleven_text_to_sound_v2
eleven_text_to_sound_v2 or eleven_text_to_sound_v3


output_format
mp3_44100_128
mp3_44100_128, mp3_44100_192, opus_48000_128, opus_48000_192, wav_44100, wav_48000


api_base_url
https://api.elevenlabs.io
Change only for an ElevenLabs data-residency endpoint, e.g. https://api.eu.residency.elevenlabs.io




For example, to switch to the v3 sound model:
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.sound_model eleven_text_to_sound_v3
And to get 48 kHz WAV files:
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.output_format wav_48000
Watch your ElevenLabs plan. The README notes that ElevenLabs documents 192 kbps MP3 for the Creator plan and above, and 44.1 kHz WAV for Pro and above. If your plan refuses a format, the tool simply reports ElevenLabs’ error back to you.
Where your sounds go and how they reach you
Every sound is saved under your Hermes home in cache/generated/audio/, with a file name built from the description, a timestamp and an ID, so nothing is ever overwritten. Each generation also adds one line to a sounds.jsonl log in the plugin’s own data folder: the prompt, length, model, format, file size and the credits ElevenLabs billed. That log stays on your machine.
Delivery depends on where you’re chatting:

Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging apps: the tool hands the agent a MEDIA: line, and the file arrives as an attachment.
MP3 (the default) plays inline on most chat apps. Ogg Opus and WAV can arrive as plain files — Telegram shows them that way.
Discord: Hermes releases after v0.22.5 send MP3 and WAV as normal attachments that play inline.
Terminal: you get the file path.
Hermes Desktop: you get a sound card (below).

So if you run Hermes on a VPS and talk to it on Telegram, you can ask for a sound from your phone and get it back in the same chat.
The sound-design skill and the free ffmpeg script
The plugin also bundles a skill called elevenlabs-sound-design. It teaches Hermes how to write good ElevenLabs prompts (based on ElevenLabs’ own prompting guide), make loops, choose a format for where the sound is going — a game engine, a video, an app interface or a chat — and build a sound pack.
Inside that skill is sfx_tool.py, a local post-processing script that uses ffmpeg. It can downmix to mono, trim silence, normalise loudness, add fades, check a loop seam for clicks, convert between OGG, WAV and MP3, and pack a named set into a folder with a manifest.json and a zip. It can also build a game “variation set” with matched loudness, such as three gravel footsteps.
The important part: this processing costs no ElevenLabs credits, because it runs on your own machine. You pay ElevenLabs once to generate a sound, then tidy it up for free. One example from the README:
python3 sfx_tool.py pack t1.wav t2.wav t3.wav --name "Footstep Gravel" --out-dir . --variations
You don’t need to run this yourself. Just ask Hermes: “Make three gravel footstep variations, mono, levelled, packed as OGG.”

Hermes Desktop: sound card and sound library
If you use Hermes Desktop, the plugin adds two things. The Desktop half is opt-in: open Capabilities → Plugins, switch to list view and turn on Desktop: ElevenLabs Sound Effects. Without it, Desktop still plays every sound in its built-in player.

Sound card: each sound shows in chat with a waveform, play/pause, a gapless loop toggle so you can hear the seam, download in each format, reveal in your file manager, and “Next” actions — 3 variations, shorter, longer, make it loop, or try the other model. Each Next row shows its cost, and nothing is billed until the agent actually runs the tool.
Sound library: press ⌘K and choose ElevenLabs: open sound library. You get every sound the active profile made, with its prompt and settings, a format filter and a prompt search. You can replay, download, reuse a prompt or jump back to the chat that made it.

The sound card needs a Hermes Desktop with tool-media renderers; the README says that arrives in the first release after v0.22.5. Older Desktops use the built-in player instead. Running Hermes on a remote machine? Install the plugin there and also into your Desktop via Capabilities → Plugins → Install from Git, with Desktop UI checked.
What it costs and what leaves your machine
Every call is a paid ElevenLabs generation on your own ElevenLabs account. The README reports what it was billed while testing: about 10 credits per second when a length is set, and a flat amount (about 50 credits) per generation when ElevenLabs picks the length. Loops can come back a little longer than requested, and the tool reports the real length next to the one you asked for. Check ElevenLabs’ own pricing for your plan.
Privacy is simple: only the sound description and its parameters are sent to ElevenLabs, with your API key. Nothing else from your conversation goes with it. Format conversions and the processing script run locally.
Who should use the Hermes ElevenLabs sound plugin
Nous framed this release as part of a “Game Dev Studio” suite, so game builders are the obvious fit. But it’s useful well beyond games:




You make…
Use it for




Games
Footsteps, pickups, UI blips, ambient loops and variation packs


Videos and Shorts
Whooshes, hits, transitions and background beds


Apps and websites
Short interface sounds in the right format


Podcasts and ads
Intros, stingers and scene sounds




If you already use Hermes for 3D work, it pairs naturally with the Meshy plugin I covered in Hermes Meshy: models from one plugin, sounds from the other, all from the same agent.
ElevenLabs sound effects vs ElevenLabs voice in Hermes
Hermes already supports ElevenLabs for text-to-speech — that’s the voice your agent speaks with. This plugin is different: it makes sound effects and music loops, not speech. The good news is they share the same key. If your ElevenLabs voice is already set up in Hermes, the installer finds ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and there’s nothing to enter.
For more on giving your agent a voice, read my guide to Hermes Apollo Voice.
My verdict on Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects
This is a tidy, well-built plugin. One tool, clear settings, a skill that knows how to prompt, and a free local script for the fiddly editing work. The Desktop sound library is a nice touch for anyone making lots of sounds. Watch your credits, start with MP3, and if you build games, videos or apps, Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects are worth installing today.

Watch your ElevenLabs plan. The README notes that ElevenLabs documents 192 kbps MP3 for the Creator plan and above, and 44.1 kHz WAV for Pro and above. If your plan refuses a format, the tool simply reports ElevenLabs’ error back to you.

Where your sounds go and how they reach you

Every sound is saved under your Hermes home in cache/generated/audio/, with a file name built from the description, a timestamp and an ID, so nothing is ever overwritten. Each generation also adds one line to a sounds.jsonl log in the plugin’s own data folder: the prompt, length, model, format, file size and the credits ElevenLabs billed. That log stays on your machine.

Delivery depends on where you’re chatting:

Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging apps: the tool hands the agent a MEDIA: line, and the file arrives as an attachment.

MP3 (the default) plays inline on most chat apps. Ogg Opus and WAV can arrive as plain files — Telegram shows them that way.

Discord: Hermes releases after v0.22.5 send MP3 and WAV as normal attachments that play inline.

Terminal: you get the file path.

Hermes Desktop: you get a sound card (below).

So if you run Hermes on a VPS and talk to it on Telegram, you can ask for a sound from your phone and get it back in the same chat.

The sound-design skill and the free ffmpeg script

The plugin also bundles a skill called elevenlabs-sound-design. It teaches Hermes how to write good ElevenLabs prompts (based on ElevenLabs’ own prompting guide), make loops, choose a format for where the sound is going — a game engine, a video, an app interface or a chat — and build a sound pack.

Inside that skill is sfx_tool.py, a local post-processing script that uses ffmpeg. It can downmix to mono, trim silence, normalise loudness, add fades, check a loop seam for clicks, convert between OGG, WAV and MP3, and pack a named set into a folder with a manifest.json and a zip. It can also build a game “variation set” with matched loudness, such as three gravel footsteps.

The important part: this processing costs no ElevenLabs credits, because it runs on your own machine. You pay ElevenLabs once to generate a sound, then tidy it up for free. One example from the README:

python3 sfx_tool.py pack t1.wav t2.wav t3.wav --name "Footstep Gravel" --out-dir . --variations

You don’t need to run this yourself. Just ask Hermes: “Make three gravel footstep variations, mono, levelled, packed as OGG.”

Hermes Desktop: sound card and sound library

If you use Hermes Desktop, the plugin adds two things. The Desktop half is opt-in: open Capabilities → Plugins, switch to list view and turn on Desktop: ElevenLabs Sound Effects. Without it, Desktop still plays every sound in its built-in player.

Sound card: each sound shows in chat with a waveform, play/pause, a gapless loop toggle so you can hear the seam, download in each format, reveal in your file manager, and “Next” actions — 3 variations, shorter, longer, make it loop, or try the other model. Each Next row shows its cost, and nothing is billed until the agent actually runs the tool.

Sound library: press ⌘K and choose ElevenLabs: open sound library. You get every sound the active profile made, with its prompt and settings, a format filter and a prompt search. You can replay, download, reuse a prompt or jump back to the chat that made it.

The sound card needs a Hermes Desktop with tool-media renderers; the README says that arrives in the first release after v0.22.5. Older Desktops use the built-in player instead. Running Hermes on a remote machine? Install the plugin there and also into your Desktop via Capabilities → Plugins → Install from Git, with Desktop UI checked.

What it costs and what leaves your machine

Every call is a paid ElevenLabs generation on your own ElevenLabs account. The README reports what it was billed while testing: about 10 credits per second when a length is set, and a flat amount (about 50 credits) per generation when ElevenLabs picks the length. Loops can come back a little longer than requested, and the tool reports the real length next to the one you asked for. Check ElevenLabs’ own pricing for your plan.

Privacy is simple: only the sound description and its parameters are sent to ElevenLabs, with your API key. Nothing else from your conversation goes with it. Format conversions and the processing script run locally.

Who should use the Hermes ElevenLabs sound plugin

Nous framed this release as part of a “Game Dev Studio” suite, so game builders are the obvious fit. But it’s useful well beyond games:

You make…

If you already use Hermes for 3D work, it pairs naturally with the Meshy plugin I covered in Hermes Meshy: models from one plugin, sounds from the other, all from the same agent.

ElevenLabs sound effects vs ElevenLabs voice in Hermes

Hermes already supports ElevenLabs for text-to-speech — that’s the voice your agent speaks with. This plugin is different: it makes sound effects and music loops, not speech. The good news is they share the same key. If your ElevenLabs voice is already set up in Hermes, the installer finds ELEVENLABS_API_KEY and there’s nothing to enter.

My verdict on Hermes Agent ElevenLabs sound effects

This is a tidy, well-built plugin. One tool, clear settings, a skill that knows how to prompt, and a free local script for the fiddly editing work. The Desktop sound library is a nice touch for anyone making lots of sounds. fix(bot-desktop): the idle stop of an abandoned human lease releases that lease

Once a human lease lapses (four windows, ten minutes at least) the screen is stopped, but lease.json still
named the human, so computer_use and the browser refused with "a human has control" before anything
started the next screen: the docs' "the next use starts it again" did not hold. After that stop the
lease is released, but only the generation judged abandoned: lease.release() takes the epoch read before
the stop and does nothing if the lease changed since, so a takeover made while the screen was stopping
(another viewer, or the same viewer handing back and taking over again) is kept, and an abandoned lease
with no viewer id never turns into a bare release.

fix(bot-desktop): a killed sleep or check no longer ends the screen's self-stop

The watch loop inherited the launcher's set -e. A sleep killed from outside (a stray pkill, the OOM
killer) made wait fail and ended the loop silently, so that screen never stopped itself again. The
loop now runs with set +e: a killed sleep goes straight to the check, a failed check retries in 300 s.
A sleep that fails on its own (it cannot sleep at all) still ends the loop rather than spinning the check.

top_items.title: Hermes Agent ElevenLabs: Make Sound Effects With the Official Plugin
top_items.content:
Hermes Agent ElevenLabs support just got a new trick: Nous Research released an official plugin called `elevenlabs-sound-effects` that lets Hermes turn a short text description into a real sound effect. You type “a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall” and Hermes makes the audio file and sends it to you in chat. The plugin (v1.2.0) was added to the Hermes plugin catalog on 26 October 2026, and Nous announced it on X the next day as part of a growing set of “Game Dev Studio” tools for Hermes. Below I cover what it does, how to install it, every setting, what it costs to run, and how it fits next to the ElevenLabs voice you may already use in Hermes. I’ve also put one of my Hermes walkthrough videos below.

Key takeaways

- One tool, elevenlabs_sound_effect: text in, sound file out (0.5 to 30 seconds, optional seamless loop).

- Install with `hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects`.

- Uses the same ELEVENLABS_API_KEY as Hermes’ ElevenLabs voice.

- Ships a sound-design skill, a free local ffmpeg script and a Desktop sound library.

- Want this working in your business? Claim a free strategy session.

## What the Hermes Agent ElevenLabs plugin does

The plugin connects Hermes to the ElevenLabs Sound Effects API. According to the catalog page, it adds exactly one tool to your agent: `elevenlabs_sound_effect`. You describe a sound in plain English and Hermes generates an audio file between 0.5 and 30 seconds long. It can also make the sound a seamless loop, which matters for things like background music, engine hums or rain.

Examples straight from the README:

- “Glass shattering on a tile floor”

- “A short retro coin pickup blip”

- “90s hip-hop drum loop, 90 BPM, loopable”

- “The sound of a heavy wooden door creaking open in a stone hall”

Hermes picks the details for each sound itself: the description (up to 450 characters — longer prompts are refused before anything is sent), the length, whether it loops, and a `prompt_influence` value from 0 to 1. A higher value follows your words more literally; a lower one gives more variety. You can also ask for a specific model on a single sound.

It’s an Official plugin, maintained by NousResearch, listed under Tools, and it needs Hermes 0.22.0 or newer. It runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, and its only Python dependency is `httpx`, which Hermes already ships.

## How to install the ElevenLabs plugin in Hermes

Installing takes one command. Here are the steps, in order:

- Make sure you’re on Hermes 0.22.0 or later ( `hermes update` if you’re not sure).

- Run `hermes plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects`. You can also install it straight from the hermes-official-plugins repo with `hermes plugins install NousResearch/hermes-official-plugins#elevenlabs-sound-effects`.

- If `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` isn’t set yet, the installer asks for it. You create a key in ElevenLabs under Profile → API keys.

- The tool only shows up for the agent once the key is set.

Two details catch people out:

- Plugins are per profile. If you run several Hermes profiles, install it on each one you want, for example `hermes -p <profile> plugins install elevenlabs-sound-effects`.

- Restricted keys need the right permission. If your ElevenLabs key is restricted, turn on the Sound Effects permission. It’s separate from the Text to Speech permission.

Prefer not to touch the terminal? Ask your agent: “Install the elevenlabs-sound-effects plugin on this profile and check the key works.”

## Hermes ElevenLabs settings explained

In Hermes Desktop, open Capabilities → Plugins and click the gear icon on the plugin. Everywhere else, use `hermes config set`. These are the four settings the README lists:

Setting
Default
Options and notes

api_key
(unset)
Stored in.env as ELEVENLABS_API_KEY

sound_model
eleven_text_to_sound_v2
eleven_text_to_sound_v2 or eleven_text_to_sound_v3

output_format
mp3_44100_128
mp3_44100_128, mp3_44100_192, opus_48000_128, opus_48000_192, wav_44100, wav_48000

api_base_url

Change only for an ElevenLabs data-residency endpoint, e.g. https://api.eu.residency.elevenlabs.io

For example, to switch to the v3 sound model:

```
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.sound_model eleven_text_to_sound_v3
```

And to get 48 kHz WAV files:

```
hermes config set plugins.entries.elevenlabs-sound-effects.settings.output_format wav_48000
```

Watch your ElevenLabs plan. The README notes that ElevenLabs documents 192 kbps MP3 for the Creator plan and above, and 44.1 kHz WAV for Pro and above. If your plan refuses a format, the tool simply reports ElevenLabs’ error back to you.

## Where your sounds go and how they reach you

Every sound is saved under your Hermes home in `cache/generated/audio/`, with a file name built from the description, a timestamp and an ID, so nothing is ever overwritten. Each generation also adds one line to a `sounds.jsonl` log in the plugin’s own data folder: the prompt, length, model, format, file size and the credits ElevenLabs billed. That log stays on your machine.

Delivery depends on where you’re chatting:

- Telegram, Discord, Slack and other messaging apps: the tool hands the agent a `MEDIA:` line, and the file arrives as an attachment.

- MP3 (the default) plays inline on most chat apps. Ogg Opus and WAV can arrive as plain files — Telegram shows them that way.

- Discord: Hermes releases after v0.22.5 send MP3 and WAV as normal attachments that play inline.

- Terminal: you get the file path.

- Hermes Desktop: you get a sound card (below).

So if you run Hermes on a VPS and talk to it on Telegram, you can ask for a sound from your phone and get it back in the same chat.

## The sound-design skill and the free ffmpeg script

The plugin also bundles a skill called `elevenlabs-sound-design`. It teaches Hermes how to write good ElevenLabs prompts (based on ElevenLabs’ own prompting guide), make loops, choose a format for where the sound is going — a game engine, a video, an app interface or a chat — and build a sound pack.

top_items.content:
OpenClaw Enterprise (OCE) is an open-source, vendor-neutral platform for running persistent AI agents inside companies with strict security needs. It was announced on 29 September 2026 in a blog post by Kevin Lin, and on 23 October OpenClaw shared a podcast interview in which Kevin explains why he built it and how to get involved. The project’s own README sums it up in one line: “Think of it as Kubernetes for agents.” Here’s what that means, what’s inside, who it’s for, and how to try it — in plain English, with the exact setup steps from the repo.

Key takeaways

- OCE = an open-source control plane for persistent agents, self-hosted on your own infrastructure.

- Built for multi-tenancy, governance and auditability.

- Harness, model and sandbox are replaceable.

- Pre-1.0: “intended for internal pilot workloads”.

- Want agents running safely in your business? Claim a free strategy session.

## What is OpenClaw Enterprise?

OpenClaw showed what a good model plus a harness built for agent work can do. But according to the announcement, real deployment of persistent agents inside organisations has stayed limited. The feedback OpenClaw kept hearing was that a stronger shared standard for security, safety and governance was needed first — and that, as a result, many IT teams simply ban agent platforms like OpenClaw.

OpenClaw Enterprise is the answer to that. The blog frames the question as how to safely deploy powerful agents in enterprise environments without weakening what they can do. OCE adds an enterprise-grade control plane on top of the OpenClaw foundation, with:

- Multi-tenancy — separate teams, each with their own agents.

- Hard security boundaries between trusted and untrusted workloads.

- Standardised agent primitives — harness, model and sandbox.

- Governance and auditability across the whole agent lifecycle.

The control plane itself is called the OpenClaw Control Plane (OCC). It’s what you use to deploy and manage Agents.

## Why “Kubernetes for agents”?

Kubernetes is the standard way companies run lots of software containers across their own servers, with one central place to deploy, manage and control them. OCE aims to do the same job for agents. The Enterprise page shows it as one control plane on your infrastructure, with Team A and Team B each running persistent agents, and each agent built from three replaceable parts: a harness, a model and a sandbox.

That last part matters. The blog says core primitives “can be swapped out with third party solutions as well as internal implementations.” So you’re not locked into one model provider or one sandbox. That’s what “vendor neutral” means here.

## Security in OpenClaw Enterprise

The blog calls security “the primary focus” of OCE. It combines four things:

- Hard boundaries between trusted and untrusted workloads

- Sandboxing

- LLM-based reviews

- Fine-grained permissions

The Enterprise page puts it as “boundaries, not just guardrails”: multi-tenancy and hard security boundaries separate workloads, while sandboxing and fine-grained permissions help define where agents can act. The team says a reference architecture showing how these protections work together is coming in the following weeks.

In the code, two packages handle much of this, according to the README’s code layout:

Path
Responsibility

packages/iam/
Identities, roles, and resource authorization

packages/audit/
Audit events and sensitive-value sanitization

apps/controller/
HTTP API, browser console, worker, and Drivers

packages/occ/
Resource lifecycle, persistence, and work queue

cmd/occ/
Go entry point for the OCC domain CLI

## Who is behind OpenClaw Enterprise?

The blog says the project “originally started at OpenAI and then was donated to the OpenClaw Foundation, where it is now an independent project and has been further developed in collaboration with Red Hat and NVIDIA.” It also says OCE is being piloted internally at companies like Red Hat and OpenAI.

In the post, an OpenAI engineer describes their internal agent triaging chat channels, tracing problems and opening fixes with full context from git, GitHub and logs. That’s the kind of persistent, deeply connected agent OCE is built to govern.

OCE runs on your own infrastructure, and the blog says it “will always be free for any organization to use.” It’s MIT licensed.

## Is OpenClaw Enterprise ready for production?

Not yet. The Enterprise page says: “Pre-1.0 software, intended for internal pilot workloads.”

The team chose to open-source it early to build in the open with the community, with a 1.0 release planned for later this year. So the right move today is a pilot: one team, a few agents, non-critical work, and close review. OpenClaw also runs bi-weekly office hours for developers, operators, security teams and organisations exploring the platform.

## How to get started with OpenClaw Enterprise

You can self-host OCE by cloning the openclaw-enterprise repo. The README offers two paths: Local Setup to run OCC on your machine, or Kubernetes Setup to install it on a cluster you already operate.

You’ll need these tools installed first:

- Docker Engine or Podman

- k3d, kubectl and Helm

- Bash and Python 3

- Go (the version in `go.mod`)

- Node.js 24.22.1 or newer

- pnpm (the version in `package.json`)

For local setup, run this from the repository root:

```
pnpm cli:build
export OCC_DEVELOPMENT_COMPUTE_DRIVER=kubernetes
export OCC_DEVELOPMENT_CONTROL_PLANE=kubernetes
export OCC_DEVELOPMENT_SANDBOX_DRIVER=none
./bin/occ dev up
```

Those exports select the Kubernetes-only profile for deploying Agents. The README warns that if you skip them, `occ dev up` starts a Compose control-plane preview that cannot deploy Agents.

Next, deploy your first Agent and send it a model request. For that step you need an OpenAI API key with access to the default model (or the override you choose). If you installed on an existing cluster, follow the repo’s guide to deploy and verify an Agent there instead.

Once that works, use Agent Presets to reuse settings: pick a preset, fill in the variables and review the copied draft in the browser console.

## OpenClaw Enterprise vs personal OpenClaw

Built for

Running many persistent agents across an organisation

A control plane (OCC) that deploys and manages Agents

The feedback OpenClaw kept hearing was that a stronger shared standard for security, safety and governance was needed first — and that, as a result, many IT teams simply ban agent platforms like OpenClaw.

  • Hard security boundaries between trusted and untrusted workloads.
  • Standardised agent primitives — harness, model and sandbox.
  • Governance and auditability across the whole agent lifecycle.

The control plane itself is called the OpenClaw Control Plane (OCC). It’s what you use to deploy and manage Agents.

Why “Kubernetes for agents”?

Kubernetes is the standard way companies run lots of software containers across their own servers, with one central place to deploy, manage and control them. OCE aims to do the same job for agents. The Enterprise page shows it as one control plane on your infrastructure, with Team A and Team B each running persistent agents, and each agent built from three replaceable parts: a harness, a model and a sandbox.

You can self-host OCE by cloning the openclaw-enterprise repo. The README offers two paths: Local Setup to run OCC on your machine, or Kubernetes Setup to install it on a cluster you already operate.

  • Docker Engine or Podman
  • k3d, kubectl and Helm
  • Bash and Python 3
  • Go (the version in go.mod)
  • Node.js 24.22.1 or newer
  • pnpm (the version in package.json)

For local setup, run this from the repository root:

```

pnpm cli:build

export OCC_DEVELOPMENT_COMPUTE_DRIVER=kubernetes

export OCC_DEVELOPMENT_CONTROL_PLANE=kubernetes
```

Next, deploy your first Agent and send it a model request. For that step you need an OpenAI API key with access to the default model (or the override you choose). If you installed on an existing cluster, follow the repo’s guide to deploy and verify an Agent there instead.

top_items.title: OpenCode Desktop Plugins: What They Are and How to Build One
top_items.content:
OpenCode Desktop plugins are new in OpenCode v2.2.0, released on 27 October 2026, and they let you add your own panels, commands and settings pages to the OpenCode Desktop app. The release notes put it simply: you can now “create, install and share Desktop plugins” — marked experimental. Until now, OpenCode plugins could extend the server and the terminal interface. Now they can change the desktop app itself. I’ll explain it in plain English first, then walk through the developer steps from the official GUI plugin docs, and finish with the other plugin changes in v2.2.0 you should know about.

Key takeaways

- v2.2.0 adds Desktop (GUI) plugins — experimental, so the API may change.

- Built with the GUI SDK `@opencode/plugin/gui`, shipped as a `./gui-experimental` export.

- Users install them like any plugin: add the package to `"plugins"` in opencode.jsonc.

- Manage them in Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

- Want AI coding agents set up for your team? Claim a free strategy session.

## OpenCode Desktop plugins in plain English

OpenCode is an open-source AI coding agent you can run in the terminal or as a desktop app. Plugins let people add features to it without waiting for the OpenCode team. Before v2.2.0, a plugin could have two parts: a server part (the agent’s logic and tools) and a TUI part (the terminal interface).

v2.2.0 adds a third part for the desktop app. The docs say a GUI plugin “adds panels, commands, settings pages, and native integrations to OpenCode Desktop.” In practice that means a plugin can now:

- Add a command to the command palette (and optionally to the composer’s `/` menu).

- Add a panel or tab next to your session.

- Add its own settings page.

- Draw small bits of UI into slots, such as the session header or a strip at the bottom of the window.

- Add native menu items or embed a web view in the window.

The release notes also list new GUI plugin APIs for toasts, dialogs, notifications, tabs, composer controls and custom UI. And there’s a new place to manage them: Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

## Experimental: what that means for you

The docs are clear: “The GUI plugin API is experimental and may change between releases.” Even the export name, `./gui-experimental`, says so.

If you’re a business owner, that means: try Desktop plugins, but don’t build anything you can’t afford to fix after an update. If you’re a developer, pin your OpenCode version while testing and re-check the docs on each release.

## How an OpenCode Desktop plugin works: setup and main

A GUI plugin can run code in two places. The docs split them like this:

Part
Where it runs
What it can do

`setup`
Every desktop app window
Panels, commands, settings pages, slots, server sources, link handlers and styles

`main`
Once, in the Electron main process
Typed Ipc contracts, native menu items, WebContentsView embeds, and Node and Electron integrations

Most plugins only need `setup`. You reach for `main` when you need something native, like a menu bar item or a direct Node integration. One file serves both: the `./gui-experimental` file default-exports `Plugin.define`, and both processes evaluate it. Window-only exports such as `Command` are undefined in the main process, so only use them inside `setup`.

Here’s the shape of the minimal example from the docs (a command that calls the plugin’s server part, plus a log line from main):

```
import { Command, Plugin } from "@opencode/plugin/gui"
import { Acme } from "./rpc"

export default Plugin.define({
  i18n: { en: { "command.open": "Open Acme" } },
  setup(ctx) {
    ctx.add(Command, () => ({
      id: "open",
      title: ctx.t("command.open"),
      run: () => void ctx.client.rpc(Acme).open({}),
    }))
  },
  main(ctx) {
    ctx.log.write("info", "acme started")
  },
})
```

## Package setup: the./gui-experimental export

A single npm package can ship server, TUI and GUI code. You add one `./gui-experimental` export beside `./tui`, and OpenCode Desktop loads it. This is the example `package.json` from the docs:

```
{
  "name": "opencode-acme-plugin",
  "type": "module",
  "exports": {
    ".": "./src/index.ts",
    "./tui": "./src/tui.tsx",
    "./gui-experimental": "./dist/gui-experimental.cjs"
  },
  "dependencies": { "@opencode/plugin": "latest" },
  "devDependencies": {
    "solid-js": "^1.9.0",
    "vite": "^7.0.0",
    "vite-plugin-solid": "^2.11.0"
  }
}
```

The GUI part doesn’t declare its own ID. It takes the plugin’s ID (the server part’s ID, or the package name if there’s no server part), and you read it as `ctx.id`. Tokens a plugin provides must use that ID as a prefix, like `acme.counter`.

## Build it with the Vite preset

The `./gui-experimental` file must be one prebuilt CommonJS file. The docs give you a Vite preset to make that:

```
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "vite"
import { gui } from "@opencode/plugin/gui/vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [gui()] })
```

Then run `vite build`. The preset compiles Solid JSX, emits one CommonJS file with every dynamic `import()` inlined (the app can’t load a second chunk), keeps the app’s shared modules, Electron and Node built-ins external, and bundles everything else.

Two options change the defaults:

- `entry` — the file that default-exports `Plugin.define`. Defaults to `src/gui.tsx`.

- `outFile` — the bundle your `./gui-experimental` export points to. Defaults to `dist/gui-experimental.cjs`.

About shared modules: the app provides some modules to every plugin at runtime, including `effect` and `@opencode/plugin/gui`. The build fails if you import other `effect/*`, `solid-js/*` or `@opencode/*` paths, because a bundled copy wouldn’t share the app’s instance. The fix the docs give: import from the shared entry, e.g. `import { Schema } from "effect"`.

## Install and share OpenCode Desktop plugins

For users there’s nothing new to learn. The docs say users install a GUI plugin “like any other plugin; there is no separate GUI install step.” Add the package to your config:

```
// opencode.jsonc
{
  "plugins": ["opencode-acme-plugin"],
}
```

Plugin options go in the same entry, e.g. `{ "package": "opencode-acme-plugin", "options": { "team": "core" } }`. The GUI part reads them as `ctx.options` — the same values the server part gets — and changing them reloads the plugin.

Sharing works the same way as other OpenCode plugins: because server, TUI and GUI code can ship from one npm package, the package is what you share. Anyone who adds its name to `"plugins"` gets all the parts it contains. Once installed, you can manage Desktop plugins from Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

## Other OpenCode v2.2.0 plugin changes

Desktop plugins are the headline, but the v2.2.0 release changes several other things plugin authors should know:

- Session instructions: plugins can attach and update keyed session instructions with `ctx.session.instructions.entry.put/list/remove`. Each change is added as a small update at the next step instead of editing the system prompt, so the prompt cache isn’t busted. Entries survive compaction and reverts and don’t start an extra model turn.

- Image and decision generation: new experimental APIs for plugins and the SDK, for image generation or decision-model workflows.

- Prompt cache TTLs: now configurable per provider and model.

- Todo tool: restored in desktop as an opt-in.

And three breaking changes:

- `@opencode/ai` root is now the Promise API. The Effect API moved to `@opencode/ai/effect`, and `@opencode/ai/promise` is removed.

- The OpenCode GitHub Action is removed. It’s no longer published; remove it from your workflows.

- TUI plugins require OpenTUI 0.7. `@opencode/plugin` now needs `@opentui/core` and `@opentui/solid` 0.7.0. Plugins on OpenTUI 0.6 fail to install until they upgrade.

## OpenCode vs Hermes: where Desktop plugins fit

I run OpenCode next to Hermes in my own setup. OpenCode is focused on coding; Hermes is a general agent you can reach from chat apps. Desktop plugins make OpenCode’s app much more customisable for teams that live in it all day. For a full comparison, read Hermes Agent vs OpenCode, and if you want free models in either, see Hermes OpenCode Zen.

## My verdict on OpenCode Desktop plugins

This is a big step for OpenCode. One package can now change the server, the terminal and the desktop app, and users install it with one line in their config. The experimental label is real, so build small and expect changes. If you or your team already use OpenCode every day, OpenCode Desktop plugins are the easiest way yet to make the app fit how you work.

top_items.content_html:
OpenCode Desktop plugins are new in OpenCode v2.2.0, released on 27 October 2026, and they let you add your own panels, commands and settings pages to the OpenCode Desktop app. The release notes put it simply: you can now “create, install and share Desktop plugins” — marked experimental. Until now, OpenCode plugins could extend the server and the terminal interface. Now they can change the desktop app itself. I’ll explain it in plain English first, then walk through the developer steps from the official GUI plugin docs, and finish with the other plugin changes in v2.2.0 you should know about.

Key takeaways

  • v2.2.0 adds Desktop (GUI) plugins — experimental, so the API may change.
  • Built with the GUI SDK @opencode/plugin/gui, shipped as a ./gui-experimental export.
  • Users install them like any plugin: add the package to "plugins" in opencode.jsonc.
  • Manage them in Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

OpenCode Desktop plugins in plain English

OpenCode is an open-source AI coding agent you can run in the terminal or as a desktop app. Plugins let people add features to it without waiting for the OpenCode team. Before v2.2.0, a plugin could have two parts: a server part (the agent’s logic and tools) and a TUI part (the terminal interface).

v2.2.0 adds a third part for the desktop app. The docs say a GUI plugin “adds panels, commands, settings pages, and native integrations to OpenCode Desktop.” In practice that means a plugin can now:

  • Add a command to the command palette (and optionally to the composer’s / menu).
  • Add a panel or tab next to your session.
  • Add its own settings page.
  • Draw small bits of UI into slots, such as the session header or a strip at the bottom of the window.
  • Add native menu items or embed a web view in the window.

The release notes also list new GUI plugin APIs for toasts, dialogs, notifications, tabs, composer controls and custom UI. And there’s a new place to manage them: Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

Experimental: what that means for you

The docs are clear: “The GUI plugin API is experimental and may change between releases.” Even the export name, ./gui-experimental, says so.

If you’re a business owner, that means: try Desktop plugins, but don’t build anything you can’t afford to fix after an update. If you’re a developer, pin your OpenCode version while testing and re-check the docs on each release.

How an OpenCode Desktop plugin works: setup and main

A GUI plugin can run code in two places. The docs split them like this:

Part

Where it runs

What it can do

setup

Every desktop app window

Panels, commands, settings pages, slots, server sources, link handlers and styles

main

Once, in the Electron main process

Typed Ipc contracts, native menu items, WebContentsView embeds, and Node and Electron integrations

Most plugins only need setup. You reach for main when you need something native, like a menu bar item or a direct Node integration. One file serves both: the ./gui-experimental file default-exports Plugin.define, and both processes evaluate it. Window-only exports such as Command are undefined in the main process, so only use them inside setup.

Here’s the shape of the minimal example from the docs (a command that calls the plugin’s server part, plus a log line from main):

```

import { Command, Plugin } from "@opencode/plugin/gui"

import { Acme } from "./rpc"

export default Plugin.define({

i18n: { en: { "command.open": "Open Acme" } },

setup(ctx) {

ctx.add(Command, () => ({

id: "open",

title: ctx.t("command.open"),

run: () => void ctx.client.rpc(Acme).open({}),

}))

},

main(ctx) {

ctx.log.write("info", "acme started")

},

})

```

Package setup: the./gui-experimental export

A single npm package can ship server, TUI and GUI code. You add one ./gui-experimental export beside ./tui, and OpenCode Desktop loads it. This is the example package.json from the docs:

```

{

"name": "opencode-acme-plugin",

"type": "module",

"exports": {

".": "./src/index.ts",

"./tui": "./src/tui.tsx",

"./gui-experimental": "./dist/gui-experimental.cjs"

},

"dependencies": { "@opencode/plugin": "latest" },

"devDependencies": {

"solid-js": "^1.9.0",

"vite": "^7.0.0",

"vite-plugin-solid": "^2.11.0"

}

}

```

The GUI part doesn’t declare its own ID. It takes the plugin’s ID (the server part’s ID, or the package name if there’s no server part), and you read it as ctx.id. Tokens a plugin provides must use that ID as a prefix, like acme.counter.

Build it with the Vite preset

The ./gui-experimental file must be one prebuilt CommonJS file. The docs give you a Vite preset to make that:

```

// vite.config.ts

import { defineConfig } from "vite"

import { gui } from "@opencode/plugin/gui/vite"

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [gui()] })

```

Then run vite build. The preset compiles Solid JSX, emits one CommonJS file with every dynamic import() inlined (the app can’t load a second chunk), keeps the app’s shared modules, Electron and Node built-ins external, and bundles everything else.

Two options change the defaults:

  • entry — the file that default-exports Plugin.define. Defaults to src/gui.tsx.
  • outFile — the bundle your ./gui-experimental export points to. Defaults to dist/gui-experimental.cjs.

About shared modules: the app provides some modules to every plugin at runtime, including effect and @opencode/plugin/gui. The build fails if you import other effect/, solid-js/ or @opencode/* paths, because a bundled copy wouldn’t share the app’s instance. The fix the docs give: import from the shared entry, e.g. import { Schema } from "effect".

Install and share OpenCode Desktop plugins

For users there’s nothing new to learn. The docs say users install a GUI plugin “like any other plugin; there is no separate GUI install step.” Add the package to your config:

```

// opencode.jsonc

{

"plugins": ["opencode-acme-plugin"],

}

```

Plugin options go in the same entry, e.g. { "package": "opencode-acme-plugin", "options": { "team": "core" } }. The GUI part reads them as ctx.options — the same values the server part gets — and changing them reloads the plugin.

Sharing works the same way as other OpenCode plugins: because server, TUI and GUI code can ship from one npm package, the package is what you share. Anyone who adds its name to "plugins" gets all the parts it contains. Once installed, you can manage Desktop plugins from Settings › Extensions › Plugins.

Other OpenCode v2.2.0 plugin changes

Desktop plugins are the headline, but the v2.2.0 release changes several other things plugin authors should know:

  • Session instructions: plugins can attach and update keyed session instructions with ctx.session.instructions.entry.put/list/remove. Each change is added as a small update at the next step instead of editing the system prompt, so the prompt cache isn’t busted. Entries survive compaction and reverts and don’t start an extra model turn.
  • Image and decision generation: new experimental APIs for plugins and the SDK, for image generation or decision-model workflows.
  • Prompt cache TTLs: now configurable per provider and model.
  • Todo tool: restored in desktop as an opt-in.

And three breaking changes:

  • @opencode/ai root is now the Promise API. The Effect API moved to @opencode/ai/effect, and @opencode/ai/promise is removed.
  • The OpenCode GitHub Action is removed. It’s no longer published; remove it from your workflows.
  • TUI plugins require OpenTUI 0.7. @opencode/plugin now needs @opentui/core and @opentui/solid 0.7.0. Plugins on OpenTUI 0.6 fail to install until they upgrade.

OpenCode vs Hermes: where Desktop plugins fit

I run OpenCode next to Hermes in my own setup. OpenCode is focused on coding; Hermes is a general agent you can reach from chat apps. Desktop plugins make OpenCode’s app much more customisable for teams that live in it all day. For a full comparison, read Hermes Agent vs OpenCode, and if you want free models in either, see Hermes OpenCode Zen.

My verdict on OpenCode Desktop plugins

This is a big step for OpenCode. One package can now change the server, the terminal and the desktop app, and users install it with one line in their config. The experimental label is real, so build small and expect changes. If you or your team already use OpenCode every day, OpenCode Desktop plugins are the easiest way yet to make the app fit how you work.

FAQ: opencode desktop plugins

What are OpenCode Desktop plugins?

They’re plugins that add panels, commands, settings pages and native integrations to the OpenCode Desktop app. They arrived in OpenCode v2.2.0 on 27 October 2026 and are marked experimental.

How do I install an OpenCode Desktop plugin?

Add the package name to “plugins” in opencode.jsonc, for example “plugins”: [“opencode-acme-plugin”]. There is no separate GUI install step.

What SDK do OpenCode GUI plugins use?

The GUI plugin SDK, @opencode/plugin/gui. Your package exposes a./gui-experimental export pointing to one prebuilt CommonJS file, built with the Vite preset from @opencode/plugin/gui/vite.

What is the difference between setup and main?

setup runs in every desktop window and adds panels, commands, settings pages, slots and more. main runs once in the Electron main process for Ipc contracts, native menus, web view embeds and Node or Electron integrations.

Are OpenCode Desktop plugins stable?

Not yet. The docs say the GUI plugin API is experimental and may change between releases, so test carefully and re-check the docs after each update.

If you've used oh-my-pi, you already know why LSP-powered editing matters: the agent stops guessing with grep and asks the language server what a symbol actually is.

Oh My Hermes now has it built in.

lsp_definition, lsp_references and lsp_rename run on the same language servers Hermes already uses, so there's nothing extra to set up. One call renames a symbol across the whole workspace, including aliases and re-exports. It leaves alone the same-named method and the word inside a log string, exactly where find-and-replace breaks things.

We A/B tested it across 8 models:
• +30% rename success overall (47 → 61 of 72)
• +75% for smaller, cheaper models (16 → 28)
• +55% on aliased and shadowed names
• ~30% fewer tokens spent

Better results and a lower bill. Smaller models get the biggest jump.

One dag-ulw request turns into a graph. Four lanes place parts in parallel, then a separate node checks the build. It catches an M.2 running at 94°C, repairs it, re-checks the same node, and only then reports verified.

That's graph engineering, and you don't wire any of it yourself. You type /dag-ulw.

What's built into the harness:
- graph runs where every node gets its own model and reasoning effort
- a full process workflow: understand → research → decide → plan → execute → verify → operate → learn
- IDE-style tools in the OMH TUI: a live lane tree with model and tokens, a HUD with cost, steer or interrupt any agent, ! shell lines, Esc Esc to rewind, codegraph for the whole repo
